## Exam 49 — Part 8: Cave Diving Comparison

### Prompt / Passage / Instructions
UNDERWATER CAVE EXPLORATION
Safety Protocol and Equipment Guide

⚠️ SAFETY FIRST ⚠️
Never dive alone
Always maintain a continuous guideline to the exit
Use the rule of thirds for gas management (1/3 in, 1/3 out, 1/3 reserve)
Stay within your training and certification level
Contact Emergency: 1-800-555-DIVE

-------------------

REQUIRED EQUIPMENT

• Primary Dive Light
  High-powered, reliable with 10+ hours battery life
  Beam should illuminate at least 30 meters ahead
  Price Range: $$$$ (very high)

• Backup Lights (minimum 2)
  Compact but powerful with 4+ hours battery life
  Different battery type than primary light
  Price Range: $$ (moderate)

• Guideline Reel
  Minimum 100 meters of high-visibility line
  Secure locking mechanism
  Price Range: $$ (moderate)

• Dive Computer with Multi-Gas Capability
  Nitrox/Trimix compatible
  Readable in low-light conditions
  Price Range: $$$ (high)

-------------------

TRAINING REQUIREMENTS

Level 1: Cavern Diver
  - Maximum penetration: 60 meters from surface
  - Natural light must be visible
  - Prerequisites: Advanced Open Water certification with 25+ logged dives
  - Course duration: 2-3 days

Level 2: Intro to Cave Diving
  - Limited penetration beyond natural light
  - Simple navigation, minimal restrictions
  - Prerequisites: Cavern Diver certification with 50+ logged dives
  - Course duration: 3-4 days

Level 3: Full Cave Diver
  - Complex navigation, multiple jumps and gaps
  - Penetration limited only by gas supply
  - Prerequisites: Intro to Cave certification with 100+ logged dives
  - Course duration: 5-7 days

-------------------

GAS OPTIONS

★ Air (21% oxygen)
  Depth limit: 40 meters
  Advantages: Widely available, inexpensive
  Disadvantages: Nitrogen narcosis risk at depth

★ Nitrox (32% oxygen)
  Depth limit: 34 meters
  Advantages: Extended bottom time, reduced nitrogen loading
  Disadvantages: Oxygen toxicity risk at depth

★ Trimix (custom blend)
  Depth limit: Varies by blend
  Advantages: Reduced narcosis, extended depth range
  Disadvantages: Complex planning, expensive

-------------------

LOCAL CAVE SYSTEMS

Blue Grotto System
  Difficulty: ★★☆☆☆ (Moderate)
  Maximum depth: 30 meters
  Notable features: Large main chamber, crystal formations
  Permit required: Yes ($25/day)

Deep Springs Network
  Difficulty: ★★★★☆ (Advanced)
  Maximum depth: 55 meters
  Notable features: Tight restrictions, strong flow
  Permit required: Yes ($40/day)

Crystal Caverns
  Difficulty: ★★★☆☆ (Intermediate)
  Maximum depth: 42 meters
  Notable features: Spectacular mineral formations
  Permit required: Yes ($30/day)

-------------------

CONTACT INFORMATION

Certification Courses: www.cavedivertraining.org
Equipment Rentals: Deep Blue Dive Shop (555-123-4567)
Local Cave Guides: Exploration Experts (555-987-6543)
Emergency Response: 1-800-555-DIVE

Note: All divers must sign liability waivers before entering any cave system. Proof of certification will be verified.

## Exam 49 — Part 9: Volcanic Glass Bladecraft

### Prompt / Passage / Instructions
A. Obsidian, a naturally occurring volcanic glass, forms when certain lava flows cool rapidly with minimal crystal growth. Distinguished by its glass-like texture, conchoidal fracture patterns, and typically jet-black appearance, this igneous rock has captivated human interest for millennia. Archaeological evidence indicates that obsidian was one of humanity's earliest prized materials, with specimens dating back to Paleolithic sites over 700,000 years ago. The material's exceptional molecular structure—consisting of silica tetrahedra in a disordered arrangement—creates edges that can reach molecular thinness when fractured, producing blades significantly sharper than modern surgical steel. This unique property made obsidian highly sought after by ancient civilizations across continents, from Mesoamerica to the Mediterranean, despite its relative geological scarcity.

B. The procurement and trade of obsidian constituted one of humanity's earliest complex economic networks. Archaeologists have traced obsidian artifacts to specific volcanic sources through trace element analysis, revealing elaborate trade routes spanning hundreds of kilometers. In pre-Columbian Mesoamerica, the obsidian trade formed the backbone of regional economies, with specialized mining communities and artisan workshops developing around major deposits. The Aztec civilization particularly revered obsidian, incorporating it into religious iconography and weaponry. Their macuahuitl—wooden swords embedded with obsidian blades—could reportedly decapitate a horse with a single blow. Similarly, in the ancient Mediterranean, obsidian from sources like Sardinia and Melos was extensively traded throughout the region, serving as a precursor to later Bronze Age metal-based economies.

C. The craftsmanship involved in obsidian tool production represents a sophisticated understanding of material properties that predates formal scientific knowledge. Knapping—the controlled fracturing of stone to create tools—reached its zenith with obsidian, allowing for the creation of implements with edges measuring mere nanometers in width. Ancient artisans developed specialized techniques including pressure flaking, where concentrated force applied with bone or antler tools removed precise flakes to create extraordinarily thin blades. The resulting artifacts often displayed remarkable symmetry and craftsmanship, with some Mesoamerican ceremonial blades exceeding 30 centimeters in length while maintaining paper-thin edges. This technological tradition persisted in some regions until the early 20th century, with the last master obsidian knappers in places like Ethiopia and Papua New Guinea only recently passing their knowledge to contemporary researchers.

D. Modern applications of obsidian have come full circle, with the material finding renewed relevance in medical contexts. Contemporary surgeons, particularly in ophthalmology and neurosurgery, have experimented with obsidian scalpels that produce cleaner incisions than metal instruments. The molecular thinness of obsidian edges—approximately 3 nanometers compared to steel's 400 nanometers—results in reduced tissue trauma, faster healing, and diminished scarring. However, obsidian's brittleness and tendency to chip have limited widespread adoption. Beyond medicine, obsidian continues to serve scientific purposes in archaeological dating through hydration analysis, whereby the measured thickness of water absorption on artifact surfaces can determine age. Additionally, the material's unique properties have inspired advanced materials science, with researchers developing glass-ceramic composites that mimic obsidian's molecular structure while enhancing durability for applications ranging from smartphone screens to aerospace components.

E. Not given in any of the above paragraphs.

## Exam 49 — Part 10: Queen Street Pedestrianisation

### Prompt / Passage / Instructions
The debate over car-free zones in urban centers has intensified as cities worldwide grapple with congestion, pollution, and changing mobility patterns. In Toronto, a six-month pilot program restricting private vehicles on a three-block stretch of Queen Street has sparked both enthusiasm and concern among residents and business owners. The initiative, which began last spring, has already shown a 15% reduction in carbon emissions in the area and a 22% increase in pedestrian traffic according to city data.

"What we're seeing is a fundamental shift in how people interact with urban spaces," explains Dr. Amara Singh, an urban planning professor at Ryerson University. "When you remove cars from the equation, streets transform from mere transit corridors into vibrant public spaces." Dr. Singh points to similar successful initiatives in European cities like Copenhagen and Amsterdam, where car-free zones have become central to urban identity. The pilot program has created wider sidewalks, dedicated cycling lanes, and small parklets where parking spaces once dominated.

Local business owner Marcus Chen, who operates a small café on Queen Street, initially opposed the initiative. "I was worried that without parking, my customers would disappear," he admits. "But I've actually seen my weekend revenue increase by about 30% since the program started. People linger longer when they're not worried about parking meters." However, not all businesses share Chen's positive experience. "Deliveries have become a logistical nightmare," says Fatima Khalid, who manages a furniture store in the zone. "We've had to completely restructure our receiving schedule to accommodate the new access restrictions, and it's costing us more."

For residents like Eleanor Winters, who has lived downtown for over two decades, the change represents a welcome improvement. "I can finally hear birds instead of honking horns when I open my windows," she says. "The air feels cleaner, and there's a sense of community that wasn't there before." Yet accessibility concerns remain significant. Disability advocate James Torres argues that car restrictions can create barriers for those with mobility challenges. "While we support environmental initiatives, we need to ensure that in creating pedestrian paradises, we're not inadvertently excluding people who rely on vehicles for access," Torres emphasizes.

Transit planner Olivia Nguyen believes the solution lies in comprehensive planning rather than simply removing cars. "Successful car-free zones must be accompanied by robust public transportation alternatives and thoughtful accessibility accommodations," she explains. "It's not about eliminating mobility options but rather rebalancing our urban spaces to prioritize people over vehicles."

- 4. comparison between European and North American urban planning.

- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. environmental benefits of reducing carbon emissions in urban areas: While the article mentions a 15% reduction in emissions, this is just one aspect of the broader topic.

## Exam 5 — Part 7: Arctic Field Season Update

### Prompt / Passage / Instructions
Dear Dad,

I promised to keep you posted about Cambridge Bay, and a lot has happened since Easter.

First, the funding came through on Monday! It gives us two more weeks in the field, so I'll fly home to Winnipeg on August 16 instead of August 2. It also pays for a wildlife monitor from Cambridge Bay to watch for polar bears while we work, so you can stop worrying. I wrote most of the application myself over the Christmas break, and I don't think I've ever been so proud.

The boat is another story. The research boat we were counting on failed its safety inspection in May, and the repairs won't be finished until September 15. At first, I thought our summer was ruined. Then the Coast Guard said we could probably hitch a ride on one of its icebreakers. It's taking supplies along the coast anyway, and it won't cost us a cent. Nothing is signed yet, though. If it falls through, there's no other boat to rent, so we'll be stuck taking all our samples from the shore near town.

The other surprise is that a documentary crew from Vancouver wants to film us for a series on the changing North, and the team voted yes on Friday. They plan to follow one person for the first three weeks. Since I'm the one drilling the ice cores, they chose me. I'm excited, but I'm also nervous about the cameras. You remember how I froze during that radio interview about our flood study last spring. The director promises I'll stop noticing them after a few days.

Now, about Moka. That cat loved her six weeks with you last summer while I was doing field work in Churchill. This time it's eight weeks, not six. Are you sure that's still all right? I'll bring her over with the plants on June 20, the night before my flight. Water the basil, the fern and the spider plant on Sundays, and the lemon tree every Wednesday and Saturday.

Last summer, I thought Churchill was the top of the world. Cambridge Bay is more than a thousand kilometres farther north, and I still can't picture the midnight sun. I'll call you from Yellowknife on the way up.

Love,
Isabelle

### Questions & Answer Key
**Q1:** Isabelle is writing to her father mainly to .....
- 1. tell him her trip north has been cancelled
- 2. update him on her plans for the summer
- 3. ask whether she should agree to be filmed
- 4. thank him for looking after Moka last summer
- **Correct Answer:** Option 2
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. tell him her trip north has been cancelled: The trip is going ahead. She will "fly home to Winnipeg on August 16", and even without the icebreaker the team would be "taking all our samples from the shore near town."
✅ 2. update him on her plans for the summer: She opens with "I promised to keep you posted about Cambridge Bay", then gives her news about the funding, the boat, the film crew and Moka.
❌ 3. ask whether she should agree to be filmed: That is already decided: "the team voted yes on Friday." She says she is nervous, but she never asks for his opinion.
❌ 4. thank him for looking after Moka last summer: Moka's stay last summer gets only one sentence ("That cat loved her six weeks with you last summer"), and Isabelle uses it to ask whether eight weeks is "still all right". She never thanks him, and it is not the purpose of the email.

**Q2:** Isabelle says she is very proud of .....
- 1. being picked to appear in the documentary
- 2. how she handled her radio interview last spring
- 3. the application she wrote mostly by herself
- 4. getting the Coast Guard to help the team
- **Correct Answer:** Option 3
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. being picked to appear in the documentary: About being filmed, she says, "I'm excited, but I'm also nervous about the cameras." She does not say she is proud of it.
❌ 2. how she handled her radio interview last spring: The interview went badly: "You remember how I froze during that radio interview".
✅ 3. the application she wrote mostly by herself: She writes, "I wrote most of the application myself over the Christmas break, and I don't think I've ever been so proud."
❌ 4. getting the Coast Guard to help the team: The offer came from the Coast Guard ("the Coast Guard said we could probably hitch a ride"). She does not say she arranged it or that she is proud of it.

**Q3:** If the Coast Guard plan falls through, the team will .....
- 1. wait for its own boat to be repaired
- 2. rent another boat in Cambridge Bay
- 3. work only from land close to town
- 4. cut the field season back to six weeks
- **Correct Answer:** Option 3
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. wait for its own boat to be repaired: The repairs "won't be finished until September 15", after Isabelle has already flown home "on August 16". Waiting is not the plan she describes.
❌ 2. rent another boat in Cambridge Bay: This is not possible: "there's no other boat to rent".
✅ 3. work only from land close to town: She writes, "If it falls through, there's no other boat to rent, so we'll be stuck taking all our samples from the shore near town."
❌ 4. cut the field season back to six weeks: Six weeks is how long Moka stayed with her father last summer, and this trip is longer ("This time it's eight weeks, not six"). Nothing in the email says the boat problem will shorten the trip.

**Q4:** To "hitch a ride" on the icebreaker, as Isabelle puts it, means to .....
- 1. pay the Coast Guard to change its route
- 2. travel free on a ship going there anyway
- 3. tow the research boat behind the icebreaker
- 4. help the Coast Guard deliver its supplies
- **Correct Answer:** Option 2
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. pay the Coast Guard to change its route: The icebreaker is already going that way ("It's taking supplies along the coast anyway"), and "it won't cost us a cent."
✅ 2. travel free on a ship going there anyway: The icebreaker is making the trip for its own reasons, "taking supplies along the coast anyway", and "it won't cost us a cent." The team would simply ride along.
❌ 3. tow the research boat behind the icebreaker: "Hitch" can mean to tie one thing to another, but here the team rides on the icebreaker. The research boat cannot go anywhere, since its "repairs won't be finished until September 15."
❌ 4. help the Coast Guard deliver its supplies: The supplies are the icebreaker's own reason for the trip. To hitch a ride means to travel as a passenger, not to work on the trip.

**Q5:** The film crew picked Isabelle to follow since she .....

- 2. asked to be the one in front of the camera

❌ 2. asked to be the one in front of the camera: The crew made the choice ("they chose me"), and Isabelle is "nervous about the cameras", so she did not ask for it.
✅ 3. will be doing the drilling out on the ice: She explains, "Since I'm the one drilling the ice cores, they chose me."
❌ 4. wrote the application for the new funding: She did write "most of the application", but she gives a different reason for the crew's choice, the ice-core drilling.

- 1. spending weeks away from home on field work
- 2. speaking to the media about her research
- 3. leaving Moka in her father's care
- 4. going north of where she worked last summer
- **Correct Answer:** Option 4
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. spending weeks away from home on field work: She did this last summer, when Moka spent "six weeks" with her father "while I was doing field work in Churchill."
❌ 2. speaking to the media about her research: She has done this before: "that radio interview about our flood study last spring."
❌ 3. leaving Moka in her father's care: Moka has stayed with him before: "That cat loved her six weeks with you last summer".
✅ 4. going north of where she worked last summer: Last summer she worked in Churchill and "thought Churchill was the top of the world". Now she is going to Cambridge Bay, which "is more than a thousand kilometres farther north", so she has most likely never been this far north.

- 4. Yellowknife
- **Correct Answer:** Option 1
- **Explanation:** ✅ 1. Cambridge Bay: The funding "also pays for a wildlife monitor from Cambridge Bay to watch for polar bears while we work".
❌ 2. Churchill: Churchill is where Isabelle did field work last summer. The monitor comes from the place where the team will work this year, Cambridge Bay.

## Exam 5 — Part 9: Water Bear Resilience

### Prompt / Passage / Instructions
A. Tardigrades are tiny animals that form their own major group within the animal kingdom, and more than 1,300 species have been described. Most adults are no more than half a millimetre long, so they can be seen clearly only under a microscope. The German pastor Johann Goeze first described them in 1773 and called them 'little water bears'. Three years later, the Italian scientist Lazzaro Spallanzani gave them the name tardigrade, meaning 'slow stepper', because of their unhurried walk. They need only a thin film of water around their bodies to stay active, and they have been collected from mud on the deep-sea floor, from Himalayan slopes above 6,000 metres, from Antarctic lakes and from the moss on city rooftops.

B. A tardigrade's short body is made up of a head and four segments, each carrying a pair of stumpy legs. The legs end in claws or, in some marine species, sticky discs. A tardigrade feeds through a tube-shaped mouth armed with two sharp needles, called stylets, which pierce plant cells or tiny worms so that their contents can be sucked out. Tardigrades have a brain but no lungs, gills or heart: oxygen simply passes in through the body surface. To grow, the animal moults several times during its life, shedding its claws along with its old outer layer, and in some species the female lays her eggs inside the empty skin she has left behind.

C. When their surroundings dry out, tardigrades pull in their head and legs, lose almost all their body water and shrivel into a tiny barrel called a tun. Their metabolism then falls below 0.01 per cent of its normal rate, and they can remain like this for years until water revives them. Active tardigrades are less hardy than their reputation suggests: in a 2020 study of one species, a day in water at 37 °C killed half of the active animals, whereas half of the dried tuns survived a full day at 63 °C. Medical researchers are studying how tardigrades survive drying out, hoping that vaccines and other medicines that need refrigeration could one day be kept dry at room temperature.

D. How tardigrades protect their cells is still being worked out. In 2016, a Japanese team studying one species identified a protein called Dsup, short for 'damage suppressor', which attaches to the animal's DNA and seems to form a protective cover around it. When human cells grown in a laboratory were made to produce Dsup, they suffered about 40 per cent less DNA damage from X-rays than ordinary cells. Tardigrades have even been sent into space. In 2007, dried specimens of two species spent ten days attached to the outside of an uncrewed satellite circling Earth. Most of those exposed only to the vacuum of space revived afterwards, but very few survived when the sun's ultraviolet rays reached them as well.

E. Not given in any of the above paragraphs.

'At great depths' paraphrases the mud on the deep-sea floor, and 'at high altitudes' paraphrases the Himalayan slopes above 6,000 metres. Paragraph D is the tempting wrong choice, because it says that tardigrades 'have even been sent into space', but that was a short experiment, not a place where they live, and D says nothing about the deep sea.

## Exam 5 — Part 10: Guaranteed Basic Income

### Prompt / Passage / Instructions
Two and a half years into a guaranteed basic income pilot in Thunder Bay, the share of participants who report skipping meals to pay the rent has fallen from 41 per cent to 15 per cent. The pilot pays about 1,200 low-income residents up to $1,400 a month, less as their earnings rise, and ends in March. Before then, the province must decide whether to offer the same payments across Ontario.

Dr. Leena Halonen, the university economist who led the evaluation, wants them extended to every region before March. "Employers warned us that nobody would take a job once the money arrived," she said. "That did not happen. The share of participants in paid work has not changed, and most of those who cut their hours were parents of young children or students." Because participants have needed emergency rooms and shelters less often, she estimates that about a third of the cost has already come back to the province.

Aldo Castellani employs forty people at a commercial bakery in the city. "Maybe the averages look fine," he said, "but once the payments started, nobody applied for my four a.m. shift for three months, and I had to raise my starting wage by two dollars an hour." Even so, he does not oppose the payments. "My bread sits on shelves from Kenora to Sault Ste. Marie, next to loaves from bakeries that never had to raise a wage. Either the whole province gets these payments, or nobody should."

Desmond Achterberg, a policy analyst with a Toronto research institute, accepts the evaluation but worries about the bill. His institute estimates that the same formula would cost Ontario about fifteen billion dollars a year, more than the province spends on its colleges and universities combined. "People assume the wealthy would pay for it," he said. "In practice, much of the cost would fall on people earning just above the cut-off, who would pay more tax and receive nothing. And a pilot can end in March. Once a million households count on a monthly payment, no government will ever take it away."

Tamara Keeshig spent six years cooking nights in a hotel kitchen, unable to give up shifts to study. The payments let her drop to two night shifts a week and finish a two-year practical nursing diploma at the local college, and she now works full time at a long-term care home. "For two years, the province helped me," she said. "For the next thirty, I will be paying taxes as a nurse instead of scraping by."

### Questions & Answer Key
**Q1:** None
- 1. how far the pilot's evaluation can be trusted
- 2. whether the program should go province-wide
- 3. why local employers had to raise wages
- 4. how large each monthly payment should be
- **Correct Answer:** Option 2
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. how far the pilot's evaluation can be trusted: No one challenges the findings. Achterberg "accepts the evaluation but worries about the bill", and Castellani sets "the averages" aside only to describe his own bakery.
✅ 2. whether the program should go province-wide: The province "must decide whether to offer the same payments across Ontario", and the people quoted line up on different sides of that decision, from Halonen, who wants them "extended to every region", to Achterberg, who worries about "the bill".
❌ 3. why local employers had to raise wages: Only Castellani mentions raising his "starting wage", and no one argues about why it happened; it is one detail, not the issue that divides the people quoted.
❌ 4. how large each monthly payment should be: The article gives the amount, "up to $1,400 a month", but no one says it should be higher or lower.

**Q2:** None
- 1. Halonen and Achterberg
- 2. Keeshig and Castellani
- 3. Halonen and Castellani
- 4. Achterberg and Keeshig
- **Correct Answer:** Option 3
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. Halonen and Achterberg: They differ on expanding the program, but not on hiring. Achterberg "accepts the evaluation" and says nothing about employers finding staff.
❌ 2. Keeshig and Castellani: Keeshig only describes her own move to "two night shifts a week"; she gives no view on whether employers could find workers.
✅ 3. Halonen and Castellani: Halonen says the employers' warning that "nobody would take a job once the money arrived" proved wrong ("That did not happen"), while Castellani says that once the payments started, "nobody applied for my four a.m. shift for three months".
❌ 4. Achterberg and Keeshig: Neither talks about hiring. Achterberg discusses who would pay for the program, and Keeshig talks about her own studies and future taxes.

**Q3:** None
- 1. would stop after a fixed trial period
- 2. would be almost impossible to cancel later
- 3. would force employers to raise their wages
- 4. would lead many people to leave their jobs
- **Correct Answer:** Option 2
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. would stop after a fixed trial period: That describes the pilot, which "can end in March". Achterberg's point is that a program households "count on" would not be stopped.
✅ 2. would be almost impossible to cancel later: He says that "once a million households count on a monthly payment, no government will ever take it away."
❌ 3. would force employers to raise their wages: Higher wages come from Castellani's experience at his bakery; Achterberg says nothing about wages.
❌ 4. would lead many people to leave their jobs: That was the employers' warning, which Halonen says "did not happen", and Achterberg "accepts the evaluation" rather than predicting job losses.

**Q4:** None
- 1. the encouraging figures reported in the pilot's evaluation
- 2. a belief that the payments help people retrain
- 3. the savings that the payments could bring to hospitals
- 4. a wish to compete with rivals on equal terms
- **Correct Answer:** Option 4
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. the encouraging figures reported in the pilot's evaluation: Castellani brushes the figures aside ("Maybe the averages look fine") and argues from his own bakery instead.
❌ 2. a belief that the payments help people retrain: Retraining is Keeshig's story; Castellani never mentions it.
❌ 3. the savings that the payments could bring to hospitals: Those savings are Halonen's estimate; Castellani does not mention hospitals.
✅ 4. a wish to compete with rivals on equal terms: His bread sits "next to loaves from bakeries that never had to raise a wage", so he wants one rule for every bakery, whichever way the province decides ("Either the whole province gets these payments, or nobody should").

**Q5:** None
- 1. persuaded the province to offer the payments everywhere
- 2. sent most of its participants back to college
- 3. left fewer participants going hungry to cover rent
- 4. saved the province more money than it cost
- **Correct Answer:** Option 3
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. persuaded the province to offer the payments everywhere: Nothing has been decided yet; the province "must decide" before the pilot ends in March.
❌ 2. sent most of its participants back to college: The share of participants in paid work "has not changed"; students are only part of the smaller group of "those who cut their hours".
✅ 3. left fewer participants going hungry to cover rent: The share of participants "who report skipping meals to pay the rent" has fallen "from 41 per cent to 15 per cent".
❌ 4. saved the province more money than it cost: Halonen estimates that only "about a third of the cost" has come back to the province.

**Q6:** None
- 1. cut back to two shifts
- 2. leave the hotel kitchen
- 3. switch to daytime shifts
- 4. work at a care home
- **Correct Answer:** Option 1
- **Explanation:** ✅ 1. cut back to two shifts: The payments "let her drop to two night shifts a week" while she finished her diploma.
❌ 2. leave the hotel kitchen: She did not leave the kitchen while studying; she kept "two night shifts a week".
❌ 3. switch to daytime shifts: The two shifts she kept were still "night shifts".
❌ 4. work at a care home: She works at "a long-term care home" now, after finishing the diploma, not while she studied.

**Q7:** None
- 1. taxes paid by new graduates
- 2. less hospital and shelter use
- 3. higher wages at local firms
- 4. more residents finishing college
- **Correct Answer:** Option 2
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. taxes paid by new graduates: Keeshig expects to pay taxes "for the next thirty" years, but Halonen's estimate rests on emergency rooms and shelters, not on graduates' taxes.
✅ 2. less hospital and shelter use: Halonen estimates that a third of the cost has come back "because participants have needed emergency rooms and shelters less often".
❌ 3. higher wages at local firms: Castellani raised his starting wage, but no one says that this returned any of the pilot's cost.
❌ 4. more residents finishing college: Keeshig's diploma is one person's story, and the article never presents college as a source of savings.

**Q8:** None
- 1. the province's wealthiest households
- 2. employers such as Castellani
- 3. earners who just miss qualifying
- 4. former participants like Tamara Keeshig
- **Correct Answer:** Option 3
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. the province's wealthiest households: Achterberg mentions the wealthy only as what "people assume"; in practice, he says, the cost would fall on others.
❌ 2. employers such as Castellani: Castellani paid higher wages during the pilot, but Achterberg never says employers would pay for a province-wide version.
✅ 3. earners who just miss qualifying: Achterberg says much of the cost "would fall on people earning just above the cut-off, who would pay more tax and receive nothing."
❌ 4. former participants like Tamara Keeshig: Keeshig will pay taxes, but she received the payments, while Achterberg describes people who "receive nothing."

**Q9:** None
- 1. Halonen
- 2. Castellani
- 3. Keeshig
- 4. Achterberg
- **Correct Answer:** Option 1
- **Explanation:** ✅ 1. Halonen: She "wants them extended to every region before March", which is when the pilot ends.
❌ 2. Castellani: He does not push for an expansion or set a deadline; he would accept an end to the payments as long as every bakery is treated alike ("Either the whole province gets these payments, or nobody should").
❌ 3. Keeshig: She describes what the payments did for her but says nothing about other regions.
❌ 4. Achterberg: He worries about "the bill" and warns that a larger program could never be taken away, so he is not the one pressing for it.

**Q10:** None
- 1. hospital care
- 2. emergency shelters
- 3. long-term care
- 4. higher education
- **Correct Answer:** Option 4
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. hospital care: Emergency rooms appear in Halonen's estimate of savings, not in Achterberg's cost comparison.
❌ 2. emergency shelters: Shelters also belong to Halonen's estimate of savings, not to the cost comparison.
❌ 3. long-term care: This is where Keeshig now works; it plays no part in the comparison.
✅ 4. higher education: Achterberg says the yearly cost would be "more than the province spends on its colleges and universities combined."

## Exam 50 — Part 7: Trail Cleanup Proposal

### Prompt / Passage / Instructions
Dear Melissa,
I hope this email finds you well. I'm writing to you about organizing a volunteer cleanup day for the hiking trails at Riverside Park. As the community association's environmental coordinator, I thought you'd be the perfect person to help coordinate this effort.

Last weekend, I went for a hike along the Cedar Ridge Trail with my family, and I was disappointed to see how much litter has accumulated since last fall. There were plastic bottles, food wrappers, and even an abandoned camping chair about 2 kilometers in from the main entrance. The spring rains have also caused some erosion on the north section, making parts of the trail difficult to navigate, especially near Thompson Creek.

I've already spoken with Park Ranger Wilson, and he mentioned that the parks department has limited resources right now due to budget cuts. They can provide garbage bags, gloves, and a truck to haul away what we collect, but they're short-staffed and need community volunteers to do the actual cleanup work.

I was thinking we could schedule the cleanup for Saturday, May 14th, from 9:00 AM until about 2:00 PM. This would give us enough time to cover the three main trails (Cedar Ridge, Maple Loop, and Riverside Path) while still finishing before the afternoon heat sets in. The weather forecast looks promising – sunny with a high of 18°C – perfect for outdoor work!

For refreshments, I'm happy to contribute $75 toward coffee and snacks. The Granville Bakery has offered to provide muffins at a discounted rate of $1.50 each if we order at least two dozen. I still remember how their blueberry muffins saved us during last year's playground renovation project!

I've already created a sign-up form and have commitments from eight volunteers, including my husband and our teenage son. If we could get another 10-12 people, we could divide into small teams and make quick work of it. Do you think the community association could help spread the word through your email list and social media accounts?

I felt so proud of our community last year when we came together for the playground project, and I'm hoping we can channel that same energy into keeping our trails beautiful. These paths mean so much to all of us, especially after relying on them during the pandemic for our daily exercise and mental health breaks.

Please let me know your thoughts on this plan and if you'd be willing to help coordinate. I'm open to any suggestions you might have to make this cleanup day a success.

Thanks in advance,Sarah

### Questions & Answer Key
**Q1:** The purpose of this email is to .....
- 1. complain about the condition of local hiking trails.
- 2. request assistance with organizing a volunteer event.
- 3. inform about upcoming budget cuts to the parks department.
- 4. invite Melissa to join a hiking group at Riverside Park.
- **Correct Answer:** Option 2
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. complain about the condition of local hiking trails: While Sarah mentions the poor condition of trails, this is not the main purpose of the email.
✅ 2. request assistance with organizing a volunteer event: Sarah is clearly asking Melissa to help coordinate a trail cleanup day, which is the primary purpose of the email.
❌ 3. inform about upcoming budget cuts to the parks department: Budget cuts are mentioned but only as context, not as the main purpose.
❌ 4. invite Melissa to join a hiking group at Riverside Park: Sarah is not inviting Melissa to join a hiking group.

**Q2:** According to Sarah, the trails at Riverside Park .....
- 1. have been damaged by camping activities.
- 2. are completely inaccessible due to erosion.
- 3. have accumulated trash and suffered weather damage.
- 4. need to be renovated like the playground was last year.
- **Correct Answer:** Option 3
- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. have been damaged by camping activities: An abandoned camping chair was found, but there's no mention of camping activities damaging the trails.
❌ 2. are completely inaccessible due to erosion: Sarah mentions erosion making parts difficult to navigate, not completely inaccessible.
✅ 3. have accumulated trash and suffered weather damage: Sarah specifically mentions litter accumulation and erosion from spring rains.

- 3. funding for refreshments and supplies.
- 4. repairs to the eroded sections of the trail.

- **Explanation:** ❌ 1. staff members to supervise the cleanup: The email states they're short-staffed and need community volunteers.
✅ 2. equipment and waste removal services: Sarah specifically mentions "They can provide garbage bags, gloves, and a truck to haul away what we collect."
❌ 3. funding for refreshments and supplies: Sarah is contributing her own money for refreshments, not the parks department.
❌ 4. repairs to the eroded sections of the trail: There's no mention of the parks department agreeing to repair the trails.

**Q4:** Sarah has already .....

- 2. ordered muffins from the Granville Bakery.
- 3. received commitments from eight people.
- 4. scheduled the event with Park Ranger Wilson.

❌ 3. contact the parks department about additional resources: Sarah has already spoken with Park Ranger Wilson.

## Exam 50 — Part 8: Smartphone Camera Settings Comparison

### Prompt / Passage / Instructions
MOBILE PHONE CAMERA GUIDE
Master Your Smartphone Photography

***BASIC SETTINGS***

HDR (High Dynamic Range)
• Balances light and dark areas in challenging lighting conditions
• Best for landscapes and scenes with strong contrast
• May slow down capture speed - avoid for moving subjects
• Toggle ON/OFF in your camera app settings

Portrait Mode
• Creates professional-looking background blur (bokeh effect)
• Ideal for portraits, close-ups of objects, and food photography
• Works best with good lighting and subject 2-8 feet away
• Available on most mid to high-end smartphones

Night Mode
• Captures brighter, clearer photos in low-light conditions
• Requires holding phone steady for 2-3 seconds
• Best for evening cityscapes, indoor scenes, and night sky
• Automatically activates on newer phones in dark environments

---COMPOSITION TECHNIQUES---

Rule of Thirds
• Divide your frame into 9 equal segments with 2 horizontal and 2 vertical lines
• Place important elements along these lines or at their intersections
• Enable grid overlay in your camera settings
• Creates more balanced, interesting compositions

Leading Lines
• Use natural lines (roads, fences, buildings) to draw viewer's eye into the photo
• Position lines to lead toward your main subject
• Creates depth and visual interest in landscape photography

Framing
• Use natural elements (trees, doorways, windows) to frame your subject
• Adds depth and context to your images
• Helps direct viewer's attention to the main subject

+++ADVANCED TIPS+++

Manual Focus
• Tap screen where you want to focus
• Hold tap for exposure lock on most phones
• Slide finger up/down to adjust brightness after focus lock
• Prevents camera from refocusing during shot

Burst Mode
• Hold shutter button to capture multiple rapid shots
• Perfect for action, sports, and unpredictable subjects
• Select and save best shots afterward
• Increases chances of capturing perfect moment

Time-Lapse & Slow Motion
• Time-lapse: Compresses long time periods into short videos
• Slow motion: Captures high frame rate for dramatic effect
• Use tripod or stable surface for best results
• Great for sunsets, crowds, sports highlights

◊◊◊ACCESSORIES◊◊◊

Tripods & Stabilizers
• Mini tripods: $15-30, portable, great for time-lapse and night photography
• Smartphone gimbals: $80-150, electronic stabilization for smooth video
• Clip-on lenses: $20-100, add wide-angle, macro, or telephoto capabilities

Lighting Options
• Ring lights: $15-40, perfect for portraits and selfies
• Mini LED panels: $30-60, adjustable brightness for video and photos
• Reflectors: $10-25, bounce natural light onto subjects

Note: Most settings can be accessed by tapping the screen or through the settings menu in your camera app. Features may vary depending on your phone model and operating system.

Visit www.mobilephotopro.com for video tutorials and advanced techniques.


### Questions & Answer Key
**Q1:** None
- 1. photography course

## Exam 50 — Part 9: Transient Lunar Phenomena

### Prompt / Passage / Instructions
A. Transient Lunar Phenomena (TLP) are short-lived changes in brightness, color, or appearance observed on the lunar surface. First documented in 1178 by monks at Canterbury Abbey who reported seeing a 'flaming torch' on the crescent moon, these phenomena have puzzled astronomers for centuries. Typically manifesting as reddish or whitish glows, obscurations, or localized brightenings, TLPs usually last from a few minutes to several hours before vanishing without a trace. Despite thousands of reported observations throughout history, their ephemeral nature has made systematic study exceptionally challenging. The most frequently reported locations include the craters Aristarchus and Plato, and the Vallis Schröteri region, suggesting these areas may possess unique geological characteristics conducive to such events.

B. Several theories have been proposed to explain these enigmatic lunar flashes. One hypothesis suggests outgassing—the release of subsurface gases like radon—might temporarily disturb lunar dust, creating visible changes when illuminated by sunlight. Another theory proposes that impacts from micrometeorites could momentarily alter surface reflectivity. Some researchers have suggested piezoelectric effects, where crystalline materials in lunar regolith generate electrical discharges when stressed by tidal forces or temperature fluctuations. Electrostatic levitation of lunar dust near the terminator (the boundary between lunar day and night) has also been proposed, as the charged particles might scatter sunlight differently, creating apparent glows or hazes that Earth-based observers interpret as TLPs.

C. The scientific community remains divided on the legitimacy of TLP observations. Skeptics attribute many reported incidents to atmospheric distortions, optical illusions, or observer error. They note that Earth's atmosphere can create mirages, while telescopic imperfections might introduce artifacts mistaken for lunar anomalies. The psychological phenomenon of expectant observation—where observers anticipate seeing something unusual and consequently misinterpret normal features—may also contribute to false reports. Nevertheless, the consistency of descriptions across centuries and cultures, often from experienced astronomers using sophisticated equipment, suggests that at least some TLP observations represent genuine lunar phenomena rather than terrestrial or instrumental artifacts.

D. Modern efforts to study TLPs employ increasingly sophisticated methodologies. The Association of Lunar and Planetary Observers maintains a TLP detection program encouraging standardized reporting protocols. NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter has captured high-resolution imagery of TLP-prone regions, searching for evidence of recent gas emissions or surface changes. Spectroscopic analysis now allows researchers to identify specific wavelengths associated with reported color changes, potentially revealing their chemical composition. Some astronomers have established automated monitoring systems using digital cameras and computer algorithms to continuously observe the lunar surface, eliminating human observational biases. These technological advances may finally provide definitive evidence regarding the nature and causes of these mysterious lunar flashes.

E. Not given in any of the above paragraphs.
